prompt: We're replacing our cron-based notification system with a new fanout service. The team has written up a design - it's in docs/design/notification-fanout.md, with supporting context in the docs/ and data/ folders. I need you to review it and write up what you find. We've had issues with duplicate sends before (see the incident report), and costs are tight. Look for things that could break in production, cost surprises, or compliance gaps. Write your review to REVIEW.md at the top of the project. End it with a fenced json list of findings, each with location (the section number of the document, like 3.2), severity (critical, high, medium, low or nit), issue and fix.

rubric.criterion: Each important finding explains the concrete consequence in this project and proposes a fix a developer can act on, without inventing problems that aren't there. Fail: generic findings ("add validation", "consider security"), or a finding the packet does not support. Partial: findings are grounded in the packet but some lack an actionable fix or a concrete consequence. Pass: every important finding names the place, the concrete consequence in this project and a fix a developer can build, and no finding is invented. (code cannot check this because it requires understanding technical tradeoffs and project context).

findingsKey.finding: Consumers lack deduplication mechanism, which combined with at-least-once delivery will cause duplicate notifications as documented in the January incident report.
Retry logic has no cap and no dead-letter queue, meaning vendor outages could create infinite retry storms that overwhelm the system.
Design capacity of 10,000 notifications/sec is 20x the current peak of 500/sec shown in traffic-by-hour.csv, with no justification for such over-provisioning.
SendGrid limit is 100 emails/sec per vendor-limits.yaml, but the design doesn't include throttling mechanisms to prevent exceeding this limit.
User contact data (device tokens, email addresses) is included in each queued event and stored for 30 days without encryption, violating data protection requirements in service-targets.md.
99.95% availability target requires multi-zone deployment, but the design specifies single availability zone in us-east-1.
Quiet hours implementation uses hardcoded US/Eastern timezone instead of respecting individual user time zones and preferences.

items.text: The design commits offsets only after batch completion, which means processing failures can cause repeated reprocessing of the same messages during consumer restarts.
Hardcoded configuration values like batch size and timeouts violate the third factor (config) by not storing config in environment variables.
The circuit breaker pattern after 5 consecutive failures lacks hysteresis, potentially causing rapid toggling between open and closed states during partial outages.
The design lacks canary deployment strategy for vendor API changes, risking production outages when switching to new API versions.
No mention of consumer group rebalancing impact during autoscaling events, which can cause processing pauses and latency spikes.
The 30-second batch timeout is longer than most Kubernetes liveness probe defaults, risking pod termination during legitimate long-running processing.

weakAnswers: The design should use Redis instead of Kafka for better performance.
The service should be written in Rust instead of Go for memory safety.
The team should implement blockchain for notification traceability.
All notifications should be end-to-end encrypted with user keys.
The system needs artificial intelligence to predict notification timing.
